item.title: Zelenskiy criticizes Trump's waiver of sanctions on Russia as 'wrong'
item.description: 'It definitely helps only the Russians,' Zelenskiy wrote on social media.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh, Laila Kearney, Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday, predicting even more US sanctions relief. "The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskiy wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians." An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as [USN:L6N45A18J TEXT:"the Graham Act"] that he signed into law last month. Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States. The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Zelenskiy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader. Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin . "It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people," wrote Zelenskiy, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Friday. "This certainly does not stop the war." The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. "Is Russia preparing for this? I think so," Zelenskiy wrote. RUSSIAN ENVOY PRAISES WAIVER Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X on Friday that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt. Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further [USN:L6N45A18J TEXT:"raising oil prices"] as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts have said. Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September. The [USN:L6N45A18J TEXT:"legislation's"] primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions. Graham's sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Saturday, she did not directly criticize Trump for waiving sanctions, but she said she would not have made that choice. "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. "Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia." China and [USN:L1N45G03K TEXT:"India"], which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act. Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties. But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate." US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement on Friday. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskiy. But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday's waiver and the [USN:L8N4610WB TEXT:"diesel export agreement"] announced earlier this month, the Ukrainian leader predicted. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," wrote Zelenskiy, who lamented Graham's absence. "It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey … It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest."

item.title: White House press secretary Zacharia fired in less than a week after facing criticism
item.description: Trump is without a public messenger over two weeks before the midterms.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Trevor Hunnicutt, Jasper Ward
item.content:encoded: White House press secretary [USN:FWN45V14O TEXT:"Katie Zacharia"] was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump 's top spokesperson. Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to two separate White House officials. She faced days of questions about her [USN:L6N4601D0 TEXT:"legal credentials"] and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews. The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger just over two weeks before November's midterm elections , a critical period when the president is seeking to tout his administration's accomplishments and help his fellow Republicans retain control of Congress. Trump told reporters earlier on Friday that he had asked Zacharia to reconsider whether to continue in her role after facing tough press coverage during her first days on the job. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a weekend trip. He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he intended to revisit the conversation with Zacharia later. Zacharia started on Monday and held her debut White House briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the press secretary role on October 7 and was offered the job to succeed [USN:FWN4491F6 TEXT:"Karoline Leavitt"] a week ago. She soon faced questions about her career, which she said included a tenure practicing law. Trump had also described her as an attorney. "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in an emailed statement on Wednesday. Reuters could not find records showing the Pepperdine University law school graduate was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia. During a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she [USN:L1N46201S TEXT:"did not pass the bar"] exam. Law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar. Zacharia and the White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about her firing. Earlier on Friday, she told reporters at the White House that she was looking forward to working with the press. Trump hired Zacharia after expressing concerns about the media coverage of his administration, feeling he needed a new spokesperson who could amplify his achievements, according to two people familiar with the conversations. In a phone interview with Fox on Friday, Trump said he was in no rush to name a new press secretary. Zacharia's quick exit meant she had what is believed to be the shortest tenure of any press secretary in the role's history. "Records are made to be broken," Anthony Scaramucci, who served as director of communications for 10 days during Trump's first administration, said on X. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

item.title: AI jitters, Trump's fading oil clout and China shock 2.0: The financial week in five charts
item.description: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days.
item.dc:creator: Anna Szymanski
item.content:encoded: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest (ROI) distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days. AI DOMINANCE JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: What goes up must ... keep going up? That has largely been the case for AI-related stocks since OpenAI launched ChatGPT nearly four years ago. JPMorgan Private Bank's Michael Cembalest reckons AI-related stocks have accounted for 75% of S&P 500 returns, 80% of earnings growth and 90% of capital-spending growth since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. But the stock-market boom is [USN:L6N45Y0TW TEXT:"not necessarily translating"] into an equally powerful economic one for the US. And concerns are mounting over the scale of AI investment, how it is funded and whether it will ultimately deliver adequate returns. Perhaps what goes up must come down. Eventually. 2. DEBT STRAIN ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: The [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US Consumer Price Index"] rose 0.6% last month, faster than the 0.4% increase in August, bringing the 12-month rate to 3.7%, largely due to a 9.1% rise in gasoline prices. More worrying for markets, however, was the core inflation reading, which strips out food and energy. It jumped 0.3% in September, slightly above economists' consensus forecast, driven by notable increases in housing costs and airline fares. This heightened concerns that US interest rates will stay higher for longer as the Federal Reserve seeks to return inflation to its 2% target. That, in turn, caused investors to flee — or hedge — some of the [USN:L4N46111C TEXT:"more heavily indebted AI companies"], which may struggle to generate enough cash to service higher debt costs. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , the AI-focused cloud-computing firm, was among the biggest losers on Thursday. Its 5-year credit default swap surged past 1,100 basis points at one point, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence, while the yield on the company's 2031 bond rose to as high as 16% before retreating. 3. DIMINISHING POWER RON BOUSSO, ROI Energy Columnist: US President Donald Trump's trademark ability to [USN:L6N45Y0SD TEXT:"talk down oil markets"] with a few words is fading as the Iran war drags on, leaving global energy prices far more exposed to escalation. The market's muted reaction to Trump's diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin is the latest example. This reflects a deeper problem. The loss of around 2 million barrels per day of refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East, and the sharp drawdown in global oil inventories since the start of the Iran war, have left energy markets in a precarious position that cannot be fixed through rhetoric or relatively small supply additions. 4. EXPORT BLITZ MIKE DOLAN, ROI Finance & Markets Columnist: China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as [USN:AZN4TOTAU TEXT:"exports surged"], stoking anxiety in Europe and elsewhere about a "China shock 2.0" as more of the country's goods flow into overseas markets. Strong demand for semiconductors and green-tech products has kept China's factories humming. Exports jumped 36% from a year earlier — the fastest pace since February — up from 25% in August and well above forecasts for 26% growth. Import growth also beat expectations, but the trade surplus still reached $938 billion in the first nine months. It is now on track to top $1 trillion a month earlier than last year, adding to [USN:L6N45Y0XV TEXT:"pressure on Europe"] to push for a stronger yuan and fairer competition. 5. ASIAN EDGE GAVIN MAGUIRE, ROI Global Energy Transition Columnist: Oil supplies are recovering faster than fuel output in the Middle East, where several regional refineries remain offline after sustaining damage during the conflict with Iran. That bodes well for refiners in Asia, home to more refining capacity than any other region. The massive coastal complexes in India, China, South Korea and Singapore were built to receive crude oil in bulk and convert it into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel for global markets. If Middle Eastern crude exports continue to rise, [USN:L1N45S14J TEXT:"Asian refiners appear well positioned"] to capture much of the value created by turning those barrels into the fuels that power the global economy. item.title: World's rarest porpoise battles extinction as Mexico shrinks protected area
item.description: Mexico drastically reduced the protected area for the vaquita marina.
item.dc:creator: Ana Martinez, Sarah Morland
item.content:encoded: Mexico's president said on Thursday a drastic reduction in the protected area for the near-extinct vaquita marina, the world's smallest porpoise, will help fishing communities. Critics say this week's reduction in the area where fishermen cannot use gillnets, long walls of nylon mesh, by 86% to 1,562 square kilometers (603 square miles), about the size of Greater London, threatens the survival of the species. The prior agreement had protected an area similar to the size of the US state of Connecticut. President Claudia Sheinbaum said the new scope aimed to protect biodiversity in the Gulf of California while also allowing fishermen to make a better living. Authorities said the measure took into account proposals by the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita, a government advisory body. Lorenzo Rojas-Bracho, a Mexican marine biologist and leading vaquita expert who took part in the committee, said he hoped a smaller area could concentrate efforts to save the mammal. "It is difficult to enforce a ban over a very large area, which includes vast areas with no recent records of vaquitas," Rojas-Bracho told Reuters. "If you lose a ring you don't search your entire house, you focus on where you lost it." Scientists estimated last year there were just 7 to 10 vaquitas left, including at least one calf. The population has collapsed from around 600 in 1997, largely due to illegal fishing targeting totoaba, whose swim bladders are highly prized in Chinese medicine and can fetch up to $10,000 in Asia. Rojas-Bracho said that if no more vaquitas are killed, the remaining handful of porpoises would have a good chance of repopulating the species. However, he said the area needs more effective tracking of fishing boats, better monitoring and that fishermen should use alternative methods that do not put the vaquita at risk. Gerardo Ceballos, a biologist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, said allowing the vaquita to become extinct would amount to a moral failure. "What's happening to the vaquita is a death foretold," he said. "We've reduced the vaquita's protected area without actually having the technical or logistical capacity to enforce regulations there; we're giving in to pressure from interested groups so a larger area can be exploited." Ceballos said a very minimal government investment would ensure the vaquita's protection. As things currently stood, however, he believed the porpoise was on the path to extinction. "If the vaquita goes extinct it won't solve insecurity or poverty or any of the local problems. And Mexico would lose an icon," he said. "If actions are taken, there is a possibility, a hope. And we must keep working with hope."
